2. **Delete 51**, one child: 84 moves up into its place. Everything under 84
   is still bigger than 38, so the tree is still a BST.

The point to land: in both cases, **one pointer in the tree changes** —
the one that used to point at the doomed node. That's the hook for the code.

Remember: `find_` returns the pointer <blue>in the tree</blue>, by reference.
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
```cpp
Node *& find_(const K & key, Node *& r) {
    if (r == nullptr) return r;
    else if (r->key == key) return r;
    else if (key < r->key) return find_(key, r->left);
    else return find_(key, r->right);
}
```

```cpp
void remove(const K & key) {
    Node *& p = ______________________;

    if (_______________) {
        if (______________________________)
            twoChildRemove(p);
        else
            zeroOneChildRemove(p);
    }
}
```
:::
::::

::: notes
```
Node *& p = find_(key, root);
if (p != nullptr)                                  // found it (else: nothing to do)
if (p->left != nullptr && p->right != nullptr)     // two children
```

The whole idea: **find it, then fix up the pointer you found.** Because
`find_` returns `Node *&`, `p` *is* the parent's `left` or `right` (or
`root` itself), not a copy. Assigning to `p` rewires the tree.

Same trick as insert on Monday: `Node *& p = find_(key, root); if (p ==
nullptr) p = new Node(key, data);`. Insert fixes up a null pointer; remove
fixes up a non-null one.
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```cpp
void zeroOneChildRemove(Node *& p) {
    Node * temp = p;
    if (p->left == nullptr) p = p->right;
    else                    p = p->left;
    delete temp;
}
```

`remove(37)`: &nbsp; `p` is 25's `right`

`remove(89)`: &nbsp; `p` is 84's `right`
:::
::::

::: notes
`p` is a reference to the parent's pointer, so reassigning it splices the
node out:

- 37 is a leaf: `p->left` is null, so `p = p->right`, which is also null.
  25's right pointer becomes null. The leaf case comes for free.
- 89 has one child: its left is null, so `p = p->right`, and 84's right
  pointer now points at 95.

`temp` keeps the old address so we can free the node *after* rewiring.
Ask: what goes wrong if we `delete p` first? (Then `p->right` reads freed
memory.)

Both the zero- and one-child cases in four lines, and **Θ(h)**: the cost is
the `find_`.
:::

How can you rearrange what's left into a BST? &nbsp; Describe as many ways as you can.

::: notes
About 3 minutes in pairs, then collect answers on the board. Expect:

1. **Hang T<sub>R</sub> under the largest key in T<sub>L</sub>**: 13 becomes
   the root, and 51's whole subtree goes on 37's right. Legal — every key in
   T<sub>R</sub> is bigger than everything in T<sub>L</sub>. Height: **6**.
2. **Hang T<sub>L</sub> under the smallest key in T<sub>R</sub>**: 51 becomes
   the root, 13's subtree goes on 40's left. Legal. Height **4** here, but
   only by luck: in general the heights add.
3. **Promote 37**, the largest key on the left (in-order **predecessor**),
   into the hole. Height **4**.
4. **Promote 40**, the smallest key on the right (in-order **successor**).
   Height **4**.

All four are correct BSTs. Which do we want? Everything costs Θ(h), and
1 and 2 can make the tree taller (heights add); 3 and 4 never do, since
only one node moves. Wrong-but-common guesses: "13 or 51 moves up" with
nothing else changed — 13 at the root would leave 25 and 37 on its left,
51 would leave 40 on its right.

We'll use the predecessor. Where is it? Go left once, then right as far as
you can. Note that 37 and 40 sit on either side of 38 in the inorder
traversal: …, 25, 37, **38**, 40, 51, …
:::

## Watch: {.smaller}

```{=html}
<iframe src="viz/bst_explorer.html?keys=38,13,51,10,25,40,84,12,37,66,89,95&step=1" width="100%" height="560" style="border: none; border-radius: 8px;"></iframe>
```

::: notes
Step mode is already on, and the tree has 40 in it. Delete 38, and press
Step at each move: the search finds 38, then walks **left once, right to
the end** to 37, copies 37 up into the root, and removes the old 37 node,
a leaf, the easy case.

Ask before each step: where does it go next?

Then keep removing the root: delete **37** (predecessor 25), then **25**.
That third one is the tricky case: go left to 13, and 13 has **no right
child**, so 13 *is* the rightmost node of the left subtree. The root
becomes 13, and 13's old node is spliced out: 10 moves up. In the code
(next slide), `rightMost_(p->left)` returns `p->left` itself, and
`zeroOneChildRemove` rewires it. No special case.
:::

```cpp
void twoChildRemove(Node *& p) {
    Node *& iop = rightMost_(p->left);
    p->key  = iop->key;
    p->data = iop->data;
    zeroOneChildRemove(iop);
}
```

```cpp
Node *& rightMost_(Node *& r) {
    if (r->right == nullptr) return r;
    else return rightMost_(r->right);
}
```
:::
::::

::: notes
`iop` = **in-order predecessor**. `rightMost_` is a find, too: it returns
the pointer *in the tree* that points at the rightmost node: 25's `right`,
here.

Copy the predecessor's key and data up into `p`'s node, then remove the
predecessor's node. It's a rightmost node, so it has **no right child**:
it's always the easy case. One call, never a chain.

Running time: down to 38, then down to its predecessor: one path, still
**Θ(h)**.
:::

## Recap {.smaller .smallcode}

A *dictionary* is a structure supporting `insert`, `find`, and `remove`.

B\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ S\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ T\_\_\_\_\_ implementation of a dictionary incurs running time \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ for all of these.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
```cpp
dict<int> myT;
myT.insert(2);
myT.insert(7);
myT.insert(15);
myT.insert(22);
myT.insert(28);
```

How many "bad" $n$-item trees are there?
:::
::::

::: notes
**Binary Search Tree** … running time **Θ(h)**.

Inserting keys in sorted order — 2, 7, 15, 22, 28 — builds a stick: every
key goes right. (Monday's list B.) Live: in the explorer, Clear and insert
them, and watch the height readout climb with n. Height $n - 1$, so every operation is $\Theta(n)$. Our
"fast" dictionary is a linked list.

"Bad" trees: any shape where every node has at most one child, like the
zig-zag. Each of the $n - 1$ links below the root goes left or right:
**$2^{n-1}$** of them.
:::

Reminder: height(T) is

- \_\_\_\_\_\_ if T is empty
- 1 + max(height(T<sub>L</sub>), height(T<sub>R</sub>)), otherwise
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
The *algorithms* on BST depend on the height ($h$) of the tree.

The *analysis* should be in terms of the amount of data ($n$) the tree contains.

So we need relationships between $h$ and $n$:

$h \ge f(n)$

$h \le g(n)$
:::
::::

::: notes
Empty tree: height **−1**.

We know find/insert/remove cost $\Theta(h)$. To say anything in terms of
$n$, we need to pin $h$ between two functions of $n$ — that's the next
slide.
:::

What is the max height ($h$) for a tree of $n$ nodes?
:::
::::

Thus: lower bound on height \_\_\_\_\_\_, upper bound on height \_\_\_\_\_\_ — good news or bad (what's the context?)

::: notes
#1: at most $2^{h+1} - 1$ nodes (perfect tree), so $n \le 2^{h+1} - 1$ and
$h \ge \log_2(n+1) - 1$: **$h = \Omega(\log n)$**.

#2: a stick has height **$n - 1$**: $h = O(n)$.

Lower bound $\Omega(\log n)$, upper bound $O(n)$. For a **dictionary**
that's bad news: the worst case is a linked list.
:::

## Your Turn {.activity}

There are 7! = **5040** ways to insert the keys 1, 2, …, 7 into an empty BST.

\

How many of them build the **perfect** tree (height 2)?

How many build a **stick** (height 6)?

\ 

Guess what fraction for each.

::: notes
About 1 minute. Take guesses. Most people guess the perfect tree is
common and sticks are rare. Then the next slide.

Answers: **80** perfect, **64** sticks. Sticks: each of the 2^(n−1) = 64
"bad" shapes from the recap is built by exactly one insertion order.
:::

## All 5040 {.smaller}

```{=html}
<iframe src="viz/bst_heights.html" width="100%" height="520" style="border: none; border-radius: 8px;"></iframe>
```

::: notes
Press **Build the trees** at n = 7: every insertion order, exactly.

80 perfect, 64 sticks: both rare. Most land in the middle, height 3 or 4.
Average 3.67.

Then n = 100, 1,000, 10,000 (1,000 random orders each). The tallest
possible height runs off the chart (99, 999, 9,999), but the trees pile
up at a few times log n: around 12 for n = 100, 21 for 1,000, 30 for
10,000. Random BSTs are short. **On average** the height is Θ(log n).

The catch: the stick isn't rare in real life. Sorted input, the most
common input there is, builds it every time.
:::

## Average case! {.smaller}

The height of a BST depends on the order in which the data is inserted into it.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;ex. &nbsp;1 3 2 4 5 7 6 &nbsp;&nbsp;vs.&nbsp;&nbsp; 4 2 3 6 7 1 5

How many different ways are there to insert $n$ keys into a tree?

Avg height, over all arrangements of $n$ keys, is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

| operation | avg case | worst case | sorted array | sorted list |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| find | | | $\log n$ | $\log n$ |
| insert | | | $n$ | $n$ |
| delete | | | $n$ | $n$ |
| traverse | | | $n$ | $n$ |

::: notes
1 3 2 4 5 7 6 builds a tall, stringy tree (height 4); 4 2 3 6 7 1 5 builds a
bushy one (height 2). Same keys, different order.

There are **$n!$** insertion orders. Averaged over all of them, the height
is **$\Theta(\log n)$** (a classic result we won't prove).

| | avg | worst | sorted array | sorted list |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| find | log n | n | log n | n |
| insert | log n | n | n | n |
| delete | log n | n | n | n |
| traverse | n | n | n | n |

**Planted error:** sorted list *find* is shown as $\log n$. It's $n$: no
binary search without random access, so you walk the list. (Sorted array
find really is $\log n$.) Ask: "one of these is wrong — which?"

So BSTs are great *on average* — but the worst case is exactly what sorted
input produces. Can we make the worst case $\log n$ too?
:::

**Idea:** &nbsp; _____________________________________________________________

The "height balance" of a tree T is: &nbsp;&nbsp; $b = \text{height}(T_R) - \text{height}(T_L)$

A tree T is "height balanced" if:

- &nbsp;
- &nbsp;

::: notes
The right one — same three keys, height 1 instead of 2.

Idea line: change insert and remove so the tree on the left can never
happen.

A tree is height balanced if
- it's **empty**, or
- **$|b| \le 1$** at the root, **and** both subtrees are height balanced.

The recursion matters: the root being balanced isn't enough. A BST that is
height balanced everywhere is an **AVL tree** — Friday's video: how to keep
it balanced as keys come and go, and why that guarantees $O(\log n)$.
:::
